paragraphs: America is the most democratic country in the world, and at the same time it is (according to reports worthy of belief) the country in which the Roman Catholic religion is making the most progress. At first sight this is surprising. Two things must be carefully distinguished here. Equality inclines people to want to form their own opinions. But on the other hand, it gives them a taste for, and an idea of, unity, simplicity, and impartiality in the power that governs society. People living in democratic ages are therefore very prone to throw off all religious authority. But if they consent to submit to any authority of this kind, they insist at least that it be single and uniform. Religious powers that do not radiate from a common center are naturally repugnant to their minds, and they can almost as easily imagine that there should be no religion as that there should be several. Today, more than in any earlier age, Roman Catholics are seen sliding into unbelief and Protestants converting to Roman Catholicism. Looked at within the bounds of the church, the Roman Catholic faith seems to be losing ground; outside those bounds, it seems to be gaining. Nor is this hard to explain. The people of our time are naturally disposed to believe. But as soon as they have any religion, they find in themselves a hidden tendency that pushes them, without their realizing it, toward Catholicism. Many of the doctrines and practices of the Church of Rome astonish them, but they feel a secret admiration for its discipline, and its great unity attracts them. If Catholicism could at last withdraw from the political animosities it has stirred up, I have hardly any doubt that the same spirit of the age that now seems so opposed to it would become so favorable as to allow it to advance greatly and suddenly. One of the most common weaknesses of the human intellect is to try to reconcile contrary principles and to buy peace at the expense of logic. Thus there have always been, and always will be, people who submit some part of their religious belief to the principle of authority, but try to exempt several other parts of their faith from its influence, and keep their minds floating at random between liberty and obedience. But I am inclined to believe that the number of such thinkers will be smaller in democratic ages than in others, and that our descendants will tend more and more to divide simply into two groups: some giving up Christianity entirely, and others returning to the bosom of the Church of Rome.
